one_liner: Small Rust (tokio) static file server and reverse proxy whose '10x faster than nginx' small-file claim does not survive a harness check.
what_it_does: A single binary (cargo install cblt, or the ievkz/cblt Docker image) configured by a KDL 'Cbltfile' of host blocks with root/file_server, reverse_proxy (round-robin or IP-hash load balancing with lb_timeout/lb_retries), redir, redirifnotcookie and tls (rustls) directives. It can also build its proxy table from Docker Swarm service labels (MODE=docker, reads /var/run/docker.sock) and reloads its config when 'cblt --reload' drops a 'reload' file that the server polls every 5 s. It is not a drop-in for nginx: different config language and a much smaller feature set (no keep-alive, no HTTP/2, no caching, no access-log format, no timeouts).
how_it_is_fast: Nothing structurally faster than nginx: a tokio multi-thread runtime with one worker per CPU, httparse request parsing, one request per connection then close, and file bodies streamed with tokio::io::copy from tokio::fs::File (thread-pool reads, no sendfile). The README gap is best explained by the listen backlog: tokio's TcpListener::bind goes through mio, which calls listen(fd, 1024), while nginx's Linux default is NGX_LISTEN_BACKLOG 511; with 'ab -c 1000' nginx's accept queue overflows and the dropped connections wait for the 1 s TCP SYN retransmit, which matches nginx's ~1.2 s median against cblt's 200 ms maximum (inferred from source, not reproduced). With 'listen 80 backlog=1024' in nginx the comparison would likely change.
when_to_use: A hobby or internal deployment that wants one small Rust binary with a readable KDL config for a few static sites plus a reverse proxy.
Docker Swarm setups where backends announce host, path, port and load-balancing policy through service labels and a tiny label-driven proxy is enough.
Serving downloads to non-browser clients (curl, scripts) that need range requests and send no Accept-Encoding header.
Reading a compact (~2k lines) tokio HTTP/1.1 server as a learning reference.
when_not_to_use: Browser-facing static sites: browsers send Accept-Encoding: gzip, which triggers an undeclared gzip body with the wrong Content-Length (see gotchas).
Internet-facing servers: no read or idle timeouts, unbounded header and body buffering, and a 10,000-permit connection semaphore make slowloris-style exhaustion easy.
High request-rate small-file serving where keep-alive, HTTP/2, sendfile or caching matter; every request opens and closes its own TCP connection.
Several TLS domains on one port: there is no SNI certificate selection, the last host's cert/key on a port wins.
Anything needing an active upstream: last commit 2025-06-04, crate 0.6.2 from December 2024, 8 open issues.

integration.form: binary crate (cargo install cblt) or Docker image ievkz/cblt
integration.dependencies: tokio (full), httparse, http, bytes, kdl 4.6, rustls 0.23 + tokio-rustls, async-compression (gzip), bollard (Docker API), clap, fdlimit, mime_guess, env_logger/tracing
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 2021 edition; no rust-version declared in Cargo.toml or on crates.io
integration.platforms: any tokio target; Docker label mode needs the Docker socket; README and Dockerfile target Linux/Alpine
integration.thread_safety: not applicable (standalone server); config swaps go through a tokio RwLock<Arc<ServerSettings>> per port
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false: different config language, HTTP/1.1 only, no keep-alive, and no equivalents for most nginx directives

gotchas: Correctness bug at HEAD (src/response.rs send_response_file, unchanged since the 'Gzip (#3)' commit e5861b5 on 10 Nov 2024): when the request's Accept-Encoding contains 'gzip' the file body is gzip-compressed but the 'Content-Encoding: gzip' header write is commented out and Content-Length stays the uncompressed file size, so browsers get an undeclared gzip stream with a mismatched length (already-compressed PNG/JPEG are gzipped too). ab sends no Accept-Encoding, so the benchmark never exercised this path.

Harness flaw behind the README table: tokio/mio bind with backlog 1024 versus nginx's Linux default of 511, under 'ab -c 1000', so nginx's ~1.2 s median looks like accept-queue overflow plus the 1 s SYN retransmit rather than serving cost; in addition the repo's benchmark/cblt Cbltfile defines only host 'example.com', and cblt answers a Host '127.0.0.1' request with a 9-byte 403 when no '*' host exists, and no raw ab output (Document Length, Non-2xx) was published to rule that out.

Host routing: without a '*' host, the raw Host header (including any ':port') must equal a configured key exactly, else 403; build_servers stores the first host on a port without its port suffix and later ones with it, so the first named host on a non-default port never matches a client's 'host:port' Host header and gets 403. With a '*' host present, it captures every request on that port.

No timeouts and unbounded buffering: socket_to_request grows its BytesMut until headers parse and the body is read fully up to Content-Length; a suffix range 'bytes=-N' with N above the file size underflows a u64 (wraps in release) and returns Content-Length N with no body; every request is logged at info level.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Only when a tiny Rust proxy driven by Docker Swarm labels is the point; for measured static or proxy throughput, statico, kawipiko or routez publish their harnesses, and for a full-featured server Caddy (Go) or Ferron (Rust) are maintained alternatives.
verified_claims_summary: The author ran 'ab -c 1000 -n 3000 http://127.0.0.1/logo.png' (23,911-byte PNG) against cblt 0.1.x and the default nginx:latest Docker image, both in Docker on a Windows laptop (the earlier run's MINGW64 'lenovo' shell; CPU not stated), and reported p50/p75/p100 of 179/194/200 ms versus 1209/1655/2146 ms, with no raw output or status counts. The same author's earlier 5 MB run, with full ab output in article-en.md, had cblt at 1956 ms median against nginx 1.27.2 at 1941 ms and Caddy at 1768 ms, so no verified win exists.
status_note: Stale since June 2025 (crate 0.6.2, December 2024), MIT-licensed hobby project that article-en.md describes as a Rust learning exercise; fine to read or run internally, but not a browser-facing nginx replacement until the gzip header bug is fixed.
